presidents.name: George Washington
trivia: First U.S. president—and the only one elected unanimously by the Electoral College (twice).
Only president who never belonged to a political party.
Set the two-term precedent by refusing a third term; the 22nd Amendment later made two terms the legal limit.
Never lived in the White House; as president he lived in New York City, then Philadelphia.
Before the presidency, commanded the Continental Army to victory in the Revolutionary War.
Appears on the $1 bill and the quarter, and is one of the four faces on Mount Rushmore.
His dentures were not wood; they were made from materials like ivory and human or animal teeth.
Led federal troops to put down the Whiskey Rebellion (1794), proving the new government could enforce taxes.
Married Martha Custis, a wealthy widow; they had no children together.
In his Farewell Address, warned Americans against permanent foreign alliances and bitter party divisions.
Pub-trivia shorthand: the first president—and the face on the $1 bill / Mount Rushmore starter pack.

presidents.name: John Adams
trivia: First president to live in the White House (he moved in November 1800).
Only Federalist ever elected president.
Father of John Quincy Adams—the first father-son pair to both become president.
Died on July 4, 1826, the same day as Thomas Jefferson and the 50th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence.
As a lawyer, defended British soldiers charged in the Boston Massacre and won most of them acquittals.
His last words were reportedly “Thomas Jefferson survives,” not knowing Jefferson had died hours earlier.
Signed the Alien and Sedition Acts, which let the government deport foreigners and punish some criticism of the government.
Kept the Quasi-War with France from becoming a declared full-scale war.
His vice president was rival Thomas Jefferson, because before the 12th Amendment the runner-up became VP.
A Harvard-educated lawyer from Massachusetts, often contrasted with Washington as shorter and more argumentative.
Pub-trivia shorthand: Washington’s VP who became president, Jefferson’s rival, and John Quincy’s dad.

presidents.name: Thomas Jefferson
trivia: First president inaugurated in Washington, D.C.
Principal author of the Declaration of Independence.
Bought the Louisiana Territory from France in 1803 for about $15 million, roughly doubling U.S. land.
Commissioned Lewis and Clark to map and explore the Louisiana Purchase.
Died on July 4, 1826—the same day as John Adams—on the Declaration’s 50th anniversary.
Founded the University of Virginia and designed its original campus at Charlottesville.
Appears on the nickel and the $2 bill, and is one of the four faces on Mount Rushmore.
Tied Aaron Burr in the 1800 Electoral College; the House of Representatives chose Jefferson after 36 ballots.
Owned enslaved people at Monticello while writing that “all men are created equal,” and fathered children with Sally Hemings.
Popularly credited with inventing the swivel chair.
Pub-trivia shorthand: Declaration guy → Louisiana Purchase guy → dies the same July 4 as Adams.

presidents.name: James Madison
trivia: First president to ask Congress for a declaration of war (the War of 1812).
Called the “Father of the Constitution” for his central role drafting it; also helped write the Bill of Rights.
Co-wrote the Federalist Papers with Alexander Hamilton and John Jay to argue for ratifying the Constitution.
Shortest U.S. president, at about 5 feet 4 inches.
During the War of 1812, British forces burned the White House and Capitol (1814).
First Lady Dolley Madison saved a famous portrait of George Washington as British troops approached.
Federalist critics nicknamed the War of 1812 “Mr. Madison’s War.”
As Jefferson’s secretary of state before the presidency, he helped carry out the Louisiana Purchase.
After the White House burned, the Madisons lived temporarily at Washington’s Octagon House.
Graduated from Princeton (then the College of New Jersey) and was among the most scholarly early presidents.
Pub-trivia shorthand: “Father of the Constitution,” War of 1812 president, White House gets burned on his watch.

presidents.name: James Monroe
trivia: First president known to ride on a steamboat.
Issued the Monroe Doctrine (1823), telling European powers not to colonize or interfere in the Americas.
Last Founding Father to serve as president.
Won reelection in 1820 with all but one electoral vote.
His mostly one-party years are remembered as the “Era of Good Feelings.”
Died on July 4, 1831—the third president to die on Independence Day.
As Jefferson’s envoy to France (with Robert Livingston), helped negotiate the Louisiana Purchase.
Acquired Florida from Spain through the Adams–Onís Treaty (1819).
Liberia’s capital, Monrovia, was named for him because the U.S. backed a colony there for free Black Americans.
Last president strongly associated with 18th-century dress like knee breeches and powdered hair.
Pub-trivia shorthand: Monroe Doctrine guy; last Founder president; “Era of Good Feelings.”

presidents.name: John Quincy Adams
trivia: First president to be photographed (a daguerreotype taken years after he left office).
First son of a president to become president (son of John Adams).
Won the 1824 election in the House of Representatives after no one won an Electoral College majority; Jackson backers called it a “corrupt bargain.”
After leaving the White House, became the first former president to serve in the U.S. House of Representatives (17 years).
As a congressman, fought the “gag rule” against anti-slavery petitions and argued the Amistad case for Africans who seized their slave ship.
As James Monroe’s secretary of state, helped write the Monroe Doctrine and acquire Florida.
Lost the 1824 popular vote to Andrew Jackson but still became president via the House.
Kept a personal diary almost continuously for nearly 70 years.
Collapsed from a stroke on the House floor in 1848 and died two days later in the Capitol.
Took early-morning swims in the Potomac River while living in Washington—sometimes without a swimsuit, according to contemporary accounts.
Pub-trivia shorthand: John Adams’s son; wins via the House in 1824; later the anti-slavery ex-president in Congress.

presidents.name: Andrew Jackson
trivia: First president from west of the Appalachians; nicknamed “Old Hickory” for toughness.
First president someone tried to assassinate (1835); both of the attacker’s pistols misfired.
Championed white male “common man” politics and expanded voting among white men without property.
Signed the Indian Removal Act (1830), which led to forced removals including the Trail of Tears.
Destroyed the Second Bank of the United States by vetoing its recharter and removing federal deposits.
Appears on the $20 bill.
Became a national hero after winning the Battle of New Orleans in the War of 1812—fought after the peace treaty was already signed.
Killed Charles Dickinson in an 1806 duel and carried bullets in his body from fights for years.
His 1829 inauguration party got so crowded and rowdy that staff moved punch outdoors to clear the White House.
Expanded the “spoils system,” giving government jobs to political supporters.
Pub-trivia shorthand: “Old Hickory,” $20 bill, Trail of Tears, kills the national bank.

presidents.name: Martin Van Buren
trivia: First president born a U.S. citizen; every earlier president was born a British subject.
Only president whose first language was not English—he grew up speaking Dutch in Kinderhook, New York.
Nicknamed the “Little Magician” for political skill; helped build the modern Democratic Party.
His term was dominated by the Panic of 1837 financial crash; opponents nicknamed him “Martin Van Ruin.”
From Kinderhook, New York; supporters’ abbreviation “O.K.” for “Old Kinderhook” is one popular origin story for the slang “OK.”
Handpicked successor of Andrew Jackson and Jackson’s former vice president.
Ran for president again in 1848 as the Free Soil Party nominee opposing slavery’s expansion.
Lost reelection in 1840 to William Henry Harrison’s “Tippecanoe and Tyler Too” campaign.
First president of Dutch ancestry.
Rose through New York’s Albany Regency political machine before national office.
Pub-trivia shorthand: Jackson’s handpicked successor; Panic of 1837; first president born a U.S. citizen.

presidents.name: William Henry Harrison
trivia: Shortest presidency in U.S. history: he died 31 days after inauguration—the first president to die in office.
Often listed among the earliest presidents photographed while in office (his term was only a month).
Gave the longest inaugural address on record (nearly two hours) outdoors in cold weather; a popular myth blames that speech for his fatal illness.
Won with the campaign slogan “Tippecanoe and Tyler Too,” pairing his Tippecanoe battle fame with running mate John Tyler.
Grandfather of Benjamin Harrison (#23)—the only grandfather-grandson presidential pair.
Became famous after defeating Native American forces at the Battle of Tippecanoe (1811).
His 1840 campaign cast him as a hard-cider, log-cabin everyman even though he came from Virginia gentry.
At 68, he was the oldest person elected president up to that time.
Last president born a British subject before American independence.
His death created the first VP succession crisis; John Tyler insisted he was fully president, not just “acting.”
Pub-trivia shorthand: “Tippecanoe”—dies after 31 days; first president to die in office.

presidents.name: John Tyler
trivia: First vice president to become president after a death in office, establishing that the VP fully takes the office.
First president to have a veto overridden by Congress.
Critics nicknamed him “His Accidency” because he became president only after Harrison’s death.
Whigs expelled him from their own party after he vetoed their national bank bills.
Only former U.S. president later elected to the Confederate Congress.
Pushed the annexation of Texas, approved near the end of his term.
Had 15 children—more than any other president.
After one bank veto, almost his entire Cabinet resigned (Secretary of State Daniel Webster stayed longer).
His second wife, Julia Gardiner, was about 30 years younger and a New York society figure.
Often the “forgotten president” between Harrison and Polk that pub-trivia players blank on.
Pub-trivia shorthand: “His Accidency”—first VP to take over after a death; annexes Texas.
